name: Đa Bút
notes: people at the site were hunter-gatherers, and fishermen, with evidence of farming both of livestock and paddy rice

name: Leang Panninge
notes: remain discovered belonging to the Toalean culture, it provides critical understanding to human culture and migration of that period

name: Kuk Swamp
notes: evidence for early agricultural drainage systems was found here; the native crop taro was grown and later bananas and sugar cane were cultivated; it is one of the places in the world where people independently developed agriculture

name: Amnya
notes: one of the oldest known fortified settlements, as well as the northernmost Stone Age fort; built by a hunter-gatherer population, significantly predates agriculture

name: Shamanka II
notes: well-preserved cemetery

name: Gobero
notes: the oldest known cemetery in the Sahara Desert

name: Adrar Bous
notes: number of sites where microlithic tools are present, along with faunal and human remains; extensive remains of ritualized feasting by specialized Tenerian cattle pastoralists

name: Takarkori
notes: rockshelter is one of two sites where the earliest evidence of plant processing in pottery has been found; the first Saharan site where ancient DNA was able to be extracted

name: Ifri Oudadane
notes: documents the shift of local inhabitants from hunter-gatherer groups to food producers; known to contain the earliest dated crop in Northern Africa, a lentil

name: Al-Khiday
notes: multi-staged cemetery that contains evidence of discrete period occupations identified through burial phases, associated goods and living floors

name: Esh Shaheinab
notes: hunting-fishing-gathering groups that can be attributed with the beginnings of pottery making in Sudan

name: Shum Laka
notes: Later Stone Age site; important to investigations of the development and subsequent diffusion of Bantu-speaking peoples

name: Wilton
notes: represents a diverse environment that could have easily supported forager groups living in this area

name: Guilá Naquitz Cave
notes: location of the earliest known evidence for domestication of any crop on the continent, Cucurbita pepo, as well as the earliest known domestication of maize

name: Chantuto
notes: large amounts of shell deposits

name: Windover
notes: muck pond where skeletal remains of at least 168 individuals were found buried; important to worldwide archaeology because of the preserved brain tissue found there as well as the extant textiles and grave goods

name: L'Anse Amour
notes: listed as oldest known First Nations funerary monument in North America

name: Morro de Arica
notes: type site for Chinchorro culture

name: Coxcatlán Cave
notes: used mostly during the Archaic period, as a shelter and gathering place during the rainy season for groups of foragers as large as 25–30 individuals; also produced domesticated plants

name: Koster Site
notes: strata contain a total of 25 distinct occupations each separated by additional layers of soil, making the site exceptionally well-preserved

name: Mollepunko Caves
notes: more than 20 carved cave paintings that show the early domestication of Camelids among other figures

name: Guitarrero Cave
notes: artifacts in an extraordinary state of preservation at the site: textiles, wood and leather tools, and basketry; early fiberwork and traces of corn cultivation nearby

name: Huaca Prieta
notes: consists of a huge mound of ash, stones, textiles, plants and shells, with some burials and constructions

name: Edakkal Caves
notes: etched petroglyphs from the Neolithic period, indicating the presence of a prehistoric settlement

name: Talheim
notes: mass grave: pit contained the remains of 34 bodies, and evidence points towards the first signs of organized violence in Early Neolithic Europe

name: Tybrind Vig
notes: first submerged settlement excavated in Denmark; contains well-preserved artefacts from the Ertebølle Culture (including fishing equipment, paddles, textiles)
